headline: SpaceX catches the top of its giant rocket

sources.title: SpaceX's Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company (The Guardian)
SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse (The Guardian)
Elon Musk's SpaceX catches Starship rocket upper stage from space (BBC News)

chunks.text: On Saturday, November 14, 2026, SpaceX {{pulled off}} something it had never done before. The top part of its giant Starship rocket, called the ship, {{came back}} from space and was caught by its [[launch tower]], a tall steel tower at the launch site. The ship [[hovered]] next to the tower. Then two huge [[mechanical arms]], [[nicknamed]] "chopsticks," [[grabbed]] it. SpaceX workers watching the flight [[cheered]].

verbs.correct: To succeed at something very hard
verbs.wrong: To forget to do something important
verbs.why: Our small team pulls off a big show every spring. She often pulls off hard tricks on her skateboard. On November 14, SpaceX pulled off something it had never done before.

verbs.wrong: To be built at a factory
verbs.why: My brother comes back from college every summer. The birds come back to the lake each spring. The top part of the Starship rocket came back from space and was caught by its tower.

chunks.text: Starship is the world's largest rocket, at 407 feet tall. Its lower part is a [[booster]] called Super Heavy, which pushes the rocket through the first minutes of flight. The booster's 33 engines {{fire up}} together at launch. The upper part, the ship, continues into space. On Friday, November 13, the rocket {{took off}} from Texas on its 15th [[test flight]]. The plan was a "double catch," with the tower catching both parts.

verbs.correct: To begin running and making power
verbs.wrong: To be cleaned with soap and water
verbs.why: The engine fires up as soon as he turns the key. Jet engines fire up before a plane leaves the gate. The booster's 33 engines fire up together at launch.

verbs.correct: To leave the ground and start flying
verbs.wrong: To be checked for safety problems
verbs.why: Our plane takes off at nine in the morning. Small planes take off from this field every day. The rocket took off from Texas on Friday, November 13.

chunks.text: The booster catch never happened. A few minutes after launch, the booster's [[control system]], the computers that steer it, {{called off}} the catch because the booster was not in the right place. Elon Musk, who runs SpaceX, said it was also [[slightly]] [[low on fuel]]. The booster {{headed out}} to sea and {{blew up}} above the water. The flight {{fell short of}} a full double catch. The ship went into [[orbit]], a path around Earth. It [[circled]] Earth 14 times in about 22 hours.

verbs.correct: To cancel something that was planned
verbs.why: The school calls off classes when it snows a lot. Coaches often call off the game when it rains hard. A few minutes after launch, the booster's control system called off the catch.

verbs.correct: To start moving toward a place
verbs.wrong: To sink slowly under the water
verbs.why: We head out to the beach early on Saturdays. The fishing boats head out to sea before sunrise. The booster headed out to sea and blew up above the water.

verbs.correct: To explode with fire and noise
verbs.wrong: To be sold to another company
verbs.why: Old gas tanks sometimes blow up in a fire. In action movies, cars often blow up. The booster blew up above the water after it headed out to sea.

verbs.correct: To fail to reach a planned goal
verbs.wrong: To be watched by a large crowd
verbs.why: Many runners fall short of their goal in their first race. Some months our sales fall short of the target. The flight fell short of a full double catch.

chunks.text: SpaceX wants a fully [[reusable]] rocket, one that can fly again and again instead of being {{thrown away}}. That could {{bring down}} the [[high cost]] of spaceflight. The head of Britain's Royal Aeronautical Society, a group of aircraft and space experts, called the ship catch a big [[step forward]]. Musk wants to {{ramp up}} test flights to one a week. NASA plans to use a [[version]] of the ship to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028.

verbs.correct: To treat something as trash after one use
verbs.wrong: To be given a new name each year
verbs.why: Many people throw away paper cups after one use. Most families throw away a lot of plastic. SpaceX wants a rocket that can fly again and again instead of being thrown away.

verbs.correct: To make a price or cost lower
verbs.wrong: To record a cost in a report
verbs.why: Solar panels bring down our power bills. Buying in large amounts brings down the price. A reusable rocket could bring down the high cost of spaceflight.

verbs.correct: To increase how often something happens
verbs.wrong: To film flights for a TV show
verbs.why: The bus company ramps up service during rush hour. Our team ramps up practice before big games. Musk wants to ramp up test flights to one a week.

mainIdea.s: SpaceX used its tower's arms to catch the upper part of its rocket for the first time. The booster was lost at sea, but the catch is a big move toward rockets that fly many times.
mainIdea.why: SpaceX pulled off its first catch of the ship on November 14. A reusable rocket could bring down the high cost of spaceflight.

mainIdea.s: SpaceX caught the top of its rocket, but the lower part was destroyed when it crashed into the launch tower. Engineers now say the tower must be rebuilt before another test.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the booster never reached the tower. Its control system called off the catch, and it blew up above the water.

mainIdea.s: SpaceX has delayed the next launch of its huge rocket after strong storms hit the Texas coast. The company says the next test flight will now take place early in the new year.
mainIdea.why: The rocket took off on November 13, and SpaceX caught the ship when it came back from space on November 14.

tf.s: SpaceX caught the top part of its Starship rocket for the first time.
tf.why: On November 14, SpaceX pulled off this catch when the ship came back from space.

tf.s: The tower caught both parts of the rocket on this flight.
tf.why: The flight fell short of a full double catch. Only the ship was caught.

tf.s: A computer system called off the catch of the booster.
tf.why: The booster's control system found that it was not in the right place and called off the catch.

tf.s: The booster blew up after it hit the launch tower.
tf.why: The booster never reached the tower. It headed out to sea and blew up above the water.

tf.s: SpaceX wants a rocket that can fly again instead of being thrown away.
tf.why: SpaceX wants a fully reusable rocket because it could bring down the high cost of spaceflight.

tf.s: Musk wants fewer test flights after losing the booster.
tf.why: Musk wants to ramp up test flights to one a week.

lines.text: Did you see that SpaceX caught part of its rocket with the tower?
I did! The top part {{came back}} from space, and two giant arms just grabbed it.
That's [[one for the books]]. They had never {{pulled that off}} before.
Wait, wasn't the plan to catch both parts?
Yes, a double catch. But the booster's computer {{called off}} its catch.
It wasn't in the right place, and Musk said it was a little low on fuel.
It {{headed out}} to sea and {{blew up}} above the water.
So they {{fell short of}} the big goal. Still, [[a win is a win]].
Right. Catching a rocket with two metal arms really is [[rocket science]].
Why does catching it matter so much?
If they can fly the same rocket again, they don't have to {{throw it away}}.
And that could {{bring down}} the cost of going to space.
Exactly. Musk wants to {{ramp up}} test flights to one a week.
One a week? That would take spaceflight to [[the next level]].
NASA also hopes to use the ship to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028.
Well, I [[can't wait]] to see what the next flight brings.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is so unusual or great that people will remember it
ex: Our team won by 40 points. That game was one for the books.

expressions.def: Used to say that a success still counts, even if it was not perfect
ex: We only won by one point, but a win is a win.

expressions.def: Used to talk about something that is very hard to understand or do
ex: Making bread is easy. It's not rocket science.
For me, doing taxes feels like rocket science.

expressions.def: A higher or better stage than before
ex: Her new coach took her tennis to the next level.

expressions.def: Used to say that you are excited about something that will happen
ex: I can't wait to see you this weekend.
The kids can't wait for summer break.
